cue: Which day are you allowed to prank people?

es.meaning: What you shout after fooling someone on 28 December, Día de los Santos Inocentes, the Spanish-speaking world's prank day. The full line runs 'inocente palomita, que te dejaste engañar'.
es.example: Le dije que habían cancelado la cena y luego le grité: ¡inocente palomita!
es.exampleTranslation: I told him dinner was cancelled, then shouted: gotcha!
es.regionNote: The prank day is shared across Spain and Latin America; the 'palomita' rhyme is especially Mexican.

it.meaning: What you say after fooling someone on 1 April, Italy's prank day. Children traditionally stick a paper fish on someone's back.
it.example: Gli ho detto che la scuola era chiusa. Pesce d'aprile!
it.exampleTranslation: I told him school was closed. April fool!

bridge.note: Same ritual, two calendars. The Spanish-speaking world plays its pranks on 28 December, the feast of the Holy Innocents, the children Herod ordered killed, which makes the jokes a dark-to-light inversion of a grim Gospel story. Italy has no December prank day and saves it for 1 April with the rest of Europe. The punchlines differ too: Spanish mocks the victim's innocence ('inocente palomita'), Italian names the day ('pesce d'aprile').

interference.es_to_it: A Mexican who pulls a prank on an Italian friend on 28 December will just be lying to them; the day carries no licence in Italy.
interference.it_to_es: An Italian who waits until 1 April to prank Mexican friends will find the day means little there; the joke window was in December.
